title: The watercraft of the world

paragraphs.text: The countless types of boat found around the world – each type adapting to environmental factors, using available construction materials, and capitalising on the successes or failures of earlier boat builders – attest to our success in water travel within our own geographical region. Economics has certainly played a role in this process. When fishing close inshore no longer provided an adequate catch to feed growing populations, more stable boats were needed to venture further offshore; when the peoples on an opposite shore could provide raw materials and utensils, it became desirable to have boats sufficiently large to trade these items.

Limited materials for construction in some areas of the world created pockets of uniquely adapted watercraft: the Inuit skin boats where no trees exist; woven reed boats; logs lashed together to form rafts. Some exist today almost unchanged from ancient prototypes, but it is a common misconception to consider such vessels primitive, when in fact they represent such a perfect balance between need and available resources.

The hazards of travelling across water have presented special problems to be overcome. Lives and boats could be lost quickly at sea, and radical innovations in boat design were usually viewed with suspicion. Nonetheless, change has been incremental, as designers continue to seek the safest, quickest and cheapest configurations, so that most boat designs have been subject to some form of modification over time.

In other fields of study – geography, ornithology, botany – committees have established standardised terminology, but there is rarely a consensus on what to call a particular boat type. Watermen themselves often take a casual approach to boat identification, perhaps merely referring to their 'boat' or '20-footer', and it is only the scholar who feels the need to be more specific. In addition, terms assigned to boats in remote areas were often given by explorers, which has not always promoted accurate classification. Though many were fascinated by the subject, they rarely had the opportunity to stay in an area for sufficient time to relate local craft to those on neighbouring coasts. What's more, if they asked a local person what their boat was called, the answer was often the equivalent of 'boat', so that the traveller, being ignorant of the local language, sometimes labelled a craft with what was essentially a generic term.

The development of serious academic interest in the ethnography of boats only really began with James Hornell, who published widely in academic journals from 1919. While many of his papers received due praise at the time, his definitive work, produced jointly with A. C. Haddon, was a three-volume study of Pacific canoes published in 1937. It is this monumental work that has enduring value. Inevitably, as the authors themselves recognised, some of their conclusions were subject to refinement based on later research, and duly amended, but this work still remains the place to begin any study of the subject. Indeed, they have had no real successors in the global comparative study of boats, for most subsequent studies have been regional, or of one group of boats.

Meanwhile, in the United States, Howard Chapelle's American Sailing Craft, an invaluable work for the specialist reader, was published in 1936. Admittedly, Chapelle has been criticised for decorating drawings with details for which there was little historical evidence, but perhaps it was these that made them so attractive. Chapelle was subsequently appointed curator of the National Watercraft Collection and it was there in the museum that he used innovative displays to publicise the history of American working vessels in a way that was accessible to the general public.

In the Baltic region, the history of research has been especially valuable. Of course, the enthusiasm with which maritime ethnographic and archaeological studies have been pursued in this part of the world is in part a manifestation of the region's geography. Baltic boat designers may not have pushed design along any more quickly than those in several other areas, but the extraordinarily wide variety of uses to which boats have been put in the Baltic does make it a particularly rich research resource. Nonetheless, it should also be acknowledged that academics from the many small, competing countries of the area have sometimes been motivated to highlight their own nation's achievements in preference to those of neighbouring countries.

The most comprehensive study of the working boats of the Baltic region was completed by Bernhard Faeroyvik and family members from the 1920s to 1940s. Faeroyvik made use of his father's experience as a fisherman to record the local names of boats and all their myriad constituent parts. He produced a remarkable compendium of information in notes and drawings that is now deposited in Bergen's Maritime Museum. The principles and methodology Faeroyvik employed had not before been used, but have subsequently become models for such studies.

By way of contrast, in Britain, further recording work was being done in the 1930s by Phillip Oak. Although valuable, the data was rather rough and sketchy and didn't cover all areas of the country. This is perhaps understandable, as the importance of working boats to society as a whole was not sufficient to ensure the preservation of any significant collection of samples at that time. However, in 1983, Eric McKee's Working Boats of Britain set new international standards in the treatment of its subject. Above all, McKee re-emphasised the essential point established by so many of the studies in this area - the boat cannot be researched in isolation. The design and materials used are obviously important, but consideration should also be given to the whole operation of watercraft: their equipment, cargoes, and the economic and social background of their use.
